<!-- BIO (Felix §3.3 "Bio" grid, 14rem_1fr; §3.4 prose measure). -->

::: {.fx-bio}
::: {.fx-bio__head}
## Bio
:::

::: {.fx-rich}
I have spent twelve years making numbers people can sign their name to, and the last four months proving it can be done with AI doing the build. The title is a description of the work, not a claim to a job: I design the analytics, I specify what correct looks like before anything is built, and I direct AI to do the build. Every module in the Cascadia portfolio carries its own evidence: known answers set before the code, tests that run on every build, and a record of what each test caught. That is the part of the craft that does not change with the tooling: data governance, specification, semantic modeling, and defining measures other people will sign their name to.

At Lowe's ecommerce arm I proposed the business intelligence function, hired its first analysts, and ran a team of six building the data warehouse and the reporting stack behind $100M+ in revenue. At Philips Healthcare I ran BI and analytics programs across 23 manufacturing sites in eleven countries, with ongoing multi-project work at fourteen of them, and 200+ stakeholders. None of those sites reported to me.

I kept my own book of work the whole time I was managing, and the portfolio is what that looks like with today's tools: ten builds in four months, each one specified, validated and operated the way I would ask a team to do it. What I am looking for now is a reporting estate that has outgrown trust and a team that wants to earn it back. Trust what you can test. The rest of this site is the test.
:::
:::

## An AI Analytics Architect owns the what and the proof, not the how.
:::

::: {.fx-opener__intro}
The job has three moves. None of them is writing the code.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<ol class="fx-tiles fx-tiles--moves">
  <li class="fx-tile">
    <p class="fx-tile__num">01</p>
    <h3 class="fx-tile__title">Specify</h3>
    <p class="fx-tile__text">Turn a business need into a precise spec: the data model, the measure definitions, the matching rules, and the invariants that must hold. Correct is defined before anything is built, so there is something to check the build against.</p>
  </li>
  <li class="fx-tile">
    <p class="fx-tile__num">02</p>
    <h3 class="fx-tile__title">Direct the build</h3>
    <p class="fx-tile__text">AI tools or an engineer do the building; either works. The job is to aim the build at the spec, not to pour the concrete. That leverage is why one person now covers ground that used to take a team.</p>
  </li>
  <li class="fx-tile">
    <p class="fx-tile__num">03</p>
    <h3 class="fx-tile__title">Verify</h3>
    <p class="fx-tile__text">Nothing ships on trust. Every number is re-derived a second, independent way and reconciled against source, and a check that disagrees stops the publish. Trust what you can test.</p>
  </li>
</ol>
<div class="fx-synthesis">
  <p>Under all three sits the part no tool does. Problems arrive as separate requests and are usually one system; the architect's work is seeing that and designing the fewest pieces that hold. AI builds whatever you specify, but it will not notice that two things are one. Conformed dimensions are the plain example: encounters, claims, eligibility and rides stop being four reporting problems and become one model with shared spines.</p>
</div>
```

::: {.fx-rich .fx-white__close}
I do not hand-write the code, and that is a choice. There are plenty of people who write code well. Specifying and verifying AI-built analytics inside a business domain is the rare skill, and it is the one this site is built to demonstrate.
:::

:::
:::

        <p class="fx-outcome__text"><strong>Built the Open Quality Notification reporting that eight factories ran on.</strong> I built the original myself, before there was a development team, sourcing from SAP directly so nothing was copied between workbooks. It scaled from one site to 8, cut about 32 hours a week of manual work, brought average closure time down 5 days, and reduced the notifications aging past 30 days by 20%. Refresh went from weekly by hand to hourly during business hours, on a cadence set by how the work actually runs rather than by how often we could run it.</p>

        <p class="fx-outcome__text"><strong>Gave three plants one set of numbers.</strong> The monthly operations report pulled from Murrysville, Böblingen and Shenzhen, each calculating the same 12 KPIs differently. I ran the initiative end to end, surfaced 6 definition misalignments and reconciled 4 of them myself, and delivered one automated Power BI report on aligned definitions. It removed about 36 hours of manual compilation a month and moved the reporting cycle from the 15th to the 5th.</p>
      </li>

        <p class="fx-outcome__text"><strong>Eliminated 100+ hours a week of manual reporting.</strong> I moved disconnected spreadsheets and point-in-time extracts into automated, governed dashboards.</p>

        <p class="fx-outcome__text"><strong>Took $80K a year out of the reporting estate.</strong> I cataloged every pipeline under the Operations umbrella, traced each to the reports it fed, measured what people actually used, and retired the dead pipelines and over-frequent refreshes.
